summary: This program builds a playlist of Song objects, sorts it by artist, then copies it into a LinkedList to show how a song can be inserted at a specific position in the list and removed from the middle again.

lines.text: LinkedList is the collection this example focuses on; it stores elements as a chain of nodes, which makes inserting and removing in the middle cheap.
The playlist starts life as an ArrayList declared through the List interface, so the code depends on the general list behaviour rather than one implementation.
Each song is created with a title, artist, genre, and energy level, and appended to the end of the list.
An enhanced for loop walks the list in order so the playlist can be printed before any sorting happens.
Comparator.comparing builds a comparator from the getArtist method, and sort rearranges the list in place into alphabetical order by artist.
forEach with a method reference is a compact alternative to writing out a loop for printing every element.
Passing an existing collection to the LinkedList constructor copies all of its elements, so the linked list starts out matching the sorted playlist.

lines.code: int insertAt = 1; // between Respect and One More Time
lines.text: Naming the position in a variable makes the later message readable and keeps the index used for insertion in one place.
The two-argument add inserts the new song at the given index and shifts everything from that point onward one place later in the list.

lines.code: int removeAt = 2; // remove what is now at index 2
lines.text: The comment matters because the insertion above changed the indexes, so index 2 no longer refers to the song it did before.
remove(int) takes the element out of the list and returns it, which lets the program report exactly which song was dropped.
